events.content_detail:
Iran’s threat to target American warships with an enhanced ballistic missile appears to mark a new and potentially more dangerous phase of the Middle East conflict, six months in. Tehran says its solid-fuel Qassem Basir missile enables it to “take action against any threat, even before it is carried out”. Reports have suggested that the Qassem Basir was the missile used in tests Iran claimed to have carried out against US warships on September 5.

Washington acknowledged an Iranian attack on its nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS George Washington and a guided-missile destroyer near the Strait of Hormuz. But it said it was unclear whether the new missile had been used and confirmed its vessels had evaded the attack. But the more assertive rhetoric coming out of the Islamic Republic suggests it is moving beyond the largely retaliatory strategy that characterised much of the war and is increasingly prepared to raise the stakes itself.

Tehran has also announced it is preparing to sign an agreement with Oman which would establish a new corridor through the Strait of Hormuz extending out into the Persian Gulf, although this has yet to be confirmed. Taken together, these developments suggest that Iran is no longer simply responding to escalation – it is increasingly trying to drive it.

Ukraine and the EU have agreed on joint steps to protect the grain corridor in the Black Sea, which Russia is trying to disrupt. The parties also discussed enhancing air defense against Russian missiles, according to a post on X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister [Andrii Sybiha](https://x.com/andrii_sybiha/status/2097341106073546818), who held a phone call with EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas on September 8.

The conversation took place immediately after a new wave of massive Russian strikes on Ukraine. Sybiha informed Kallas about the consequences of the attacks and emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs to strengthen its air defense, particularly against ballistic missiles.

The minister thanked her for the substantive discussion at the recent informal meeting of EU foreign ministers and called for translating these talks into concrete decisions that match the scale of the threat.

Separately, the ministers discussed Russia's attempts to disrupt the operation of Ukraine's maritime corridor. Sybiha

### Abstract

Waging modern war requires assured access to strategic minerals and the ability to process them into products that can readily enter the supply chain. Nations planning for future conflict can defeat rivals by preventing them from accessing ready sources of minerals, employing trade bans on vital minerals and metals, and through dominating refining processes. When supply chains are broken, munitions depth is a challenge. When war is waged without domestic production capacity and assured logistics, resilience and sustainment are at risk.
